The Dog Comes on Fridays
The dog comes every Friday. One week, he comes alone.
A librarian, a dog trainer, and a dog who keeps delivering the wrong shoes to the right door. Eight Fridays to say it without an excuse.

Every Friday at six, Miles Avery trains a nervous beagle on the second floor, and every Friday his dog Toast slips upstairs to sit outside Ben Okafor's door. This week Toast brings two shoes that belong to nobody in 4B, and two men who have built a whole acquaintance out of handing back a dog run out of things to hand back. You decide what Ben says out loud, and whether a Friday walk ever gets to be called a date.
The neighbor across the landing in 4D — owner of the left shoe, and the only witness to every Friday so far.
If nobody asks, Ben and Miles stay two polite men passing a dog back and forth across a doorway forever.

Two Wrong Shoes
Get two stolen shoes back where they belong
Ben's doorway, 4B
Friday, 6:10 PM
Fourth floor. For the fifth Friday running, a toast-colored mutt is sitting outside 4B. This time he has brought gifts: a left running shoe and a right suede boot.
I open the door, look down, and do the math. Two shoes. Two different people. Zero of them me.
That's not even my size.
I take the stairs two at a time, leash in hand, already apologizing to the general area.
He believes in you.
He believes in theft. And the left one smells like a marathon nobody finished.
Five Fridays. Maybe nine sentences between us. I've rehearsed most of them in the shower.
I can take them back. Or — you probably know whose doors these are.
What does Ben do with the shoes?
Knock on doors with him.
The boot is Mrs. Pruitt, 3C. The runner is 4D. Come on. I'll introduce you as the accomplice.
Mrs. Pruitt takes her boot back and asks Miles, loudly, if he's single. 4D isn't home; they leave the runner on the mat with a note.
You know everybody's shoes.
I know everybody's late fees. Shoes are adjacent.
Ben and Miles returned both shoes together, door to door; 4D's runner was left on the mat with a note.
Return them yourself. Keep it to the doorway.
I'll get them home. You get him home.
I clip the leash on and don't argue. At the top of the stairs, I look back once.
Same time next week, probably. He's very consistent.
Ben returns the boot to 3C and leaves 4D's runner on its mat with a note that says SORRY in block capitals.
Ben returned the shoes alone and kept it to the doorway; Miles said Toast would probably be back next Friday.
Hand them back. Close the door kindly.
They're his finds. I think the finder handles returns.
Fair. That's actually in the training manual.
I take both shoes, thank him, and lead Toast down. Toast sighs at every step like I've ruined something.
4B's door clicks shut. Behind it, Ben stands very still for a full minute.
Ben handed the shoes back and closed the door; Miles returned them himself.
The Good Coat
Take Toast on one proper walk together
Linden Park, the muddy loop

He needs a long walk, and I need a witness. Linden Park?

I was talking to the dog.

Toast answers by shaking a pint of mud onto Ben's hem. Miles looks at the coat, then at Ben, longer than a trainer needs to.
I wore the good coat.
For the mud?
What does Ben tell him?
Say it: for the guy pretending it's about mud.
For the guy pretending this is about the mud.

Without him?
Without an excuse.

He's boarding next Friday. I was going to ask if I could come by anyway.

Without an excuse.

Without him?
Without an excuse.

Answer an invitation that doesn't come with a dog
Ben's door, 4B
Friday, 6:00 PM

Yes.

The front stoop of Ben's building
Saturday, 10:00 AM

Right is mine. Past the Maple Street branch, the book drop, a café that lets you sit two hours on one tea.

It goes under my window.

Which way does Ben walk?
Take his loop — the park, minus the work.
Left. I want to see it when you're not counting anyone's steps.

A Crooked Photo
Take — or don't take — one photo of the two of them
Linden Park, the bench
Sunday, 3:40 PM, a week later
Toast is home from boarding and has not forgiven Miles. He leans his entire weight against Ben's shins instead.
I want a picture. The first one where nobody's returning anything.
Miles props his phone on the bench arm and sets a ten-second timer. At three, Toast hears a squirrel thinking and launches.
The photo: a blur of tail across the frame. Ben laughing, one eye shut. Miles not looking at the camera at all. Looking at Ben.
The dog has excellent timing. Terrible composition.
He wasn't looking at the lens. He was looking at me. And now there's a timestamp.
Just us, or can I post it?
Or we try again. I can make him sit. That's literally my job.
What does Ben want to do with the photo?
Retake it — both of you looking this time.
Again. This time I want to be looking at you too, and I want the evidence.
I put Toast in a down-stay that would make my old mentor weep. Timer. Ten seconds. I don't look at the lens this time either.
The second photo is level and sharp. Both men are turned toward each other. Toast lies perfectly still at their feet, deeply offended.
Ben asked to retake the photo; in the second one they're looking at each other, Toast holding a down-stay.
Keep the crooked one. It's the good one.
Keep that one. It's the only honest photo anyone's ever taken of me.
